subject: industrial-systems
audience: FE Industrial & Systems candidates and industrial engineering students
title: The Shorter Layout That Moved More Material
featured_title: THE SHORTER LAYOUT THAT MOVED MORE MATERIAL

presentation.challenge: Layout A had the shorter average distance, but its busiest material-flow pair was much farther apart. Weighted load-distance made Layout B the better design.

practice.primary_question: How should material flow and travel distance be combined when comparing facility layouts?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Comparing layouts using only average physical distance and ignoring that high-flow department pairs should carry greater weight.
also_relevant_to: Manufacturing, Service, and Other Production Systems

case_dna.target_misconception: The layout with the lower unweighted average department distance must have the lower material-handling burden.
case_dna.why_plausible: A shorter average distance sounds efficient, but it treats low-flow and high-flow department pairs as equally important.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Layout A has distances 30, 5, and 5 ft for flows 50, 10, and 10 loads/day, giving 1600 load-ft/day. Layout B has distances 20, 15, and 15 ft, giving 1300 load-ft/day.
case_dna.corrected_model: Use a load-distance score by multiplying each pair's flow by its travel distance and summing across all relevant pairs.

problem_statement: Three department pairs have daily material flows AB=50, AC=10, and BC=10 loads/day. Layout A has pair distances AB=30 ft, AC=5 ft, BC=5 ft. Layout B has distances AB=20 ft, AC=15 ft, BC=15 ft. A note chooses Layout A because its unweighted average distance is lower. Using load-distance score, determine the better layout and the percent reduction relative to Layout A.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The shorter average distance was not the lower handling burden.
gates.prompt: Which department pair should dominate the comparison?

options.label: Use Σ(flow×distance)
options.reason: Load-distance weights each travel distance by how frequently material moves along that pair.

options.label: Use the simple average of pair distances
options.reason: That gives the same importance to high-flow and low-flow pairs.

options.label: Choose the layout with the single shortest pair distance
options.reason: One short pair does not represent total material movement.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Score both layouts
gates.result: Layout B has the lower load-distance score at 1300 load-ft/day.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the layout scores
gates.success: Layout B=1300 load-ft/day; Layout A=1600 load-ft/day.
gates.hint: Multiply each pair distance by its corresponding daily flow.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The busiest pair controls the outcome

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the layout-selection note
report: C1. Layout A has a lower simple average distance.
C2. AB carries five times the flow of AC or BC.
C3. Therefore Layout A must have the lower material-handling burden.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: The unweighted average distance is indeed lower for Layout A.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: This is the stated flow pattern.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It ignores that the longest distance in Layout A is assigned to the highest-flow pair.

evidence_choices.label: Layout A=1600 versus Layout B=1300 load-ft/day
evidence_choices.reason: The weighted score directly represents the stated material-flow burden.

correction.template: Layout {layout} is preferred at {score} load-ft/day, an {reduction}% reduction from Layout A.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reduce Layout B handling by another 10%
gates.constraint: Keep all flows and AC/BC distances unchanged.

options.label: Reduce AB distance to 17.4 ft or less
options.reason: A 10% reduction target is 1170 load-ft/day; 50d+300=1170 gives d=17.4 ft.

options.label: Reduce AB distance only to 18 ft
options.reason: That gives 1200 load-ft/day, which is less than a 10% reduction from 1300.

options.label: Keep AB at 20 ft
options.reason: That leaves the score unchanged at 1300.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply load-distance to a new layout
gates.prompt: Flows are 20 and 40 loads/day over distances 25 and 10 ft. What is total load-distance?

options.label: 95 load-ft/day
options.reason: That adds flows and distances instead of multiplying corresponding pairs.

options.label: 700 load-ft/day
options.reason: That does not match the pairwise weighted total.

gates.explanation: Load-distance is the sum of each flow multiplied by its associated travel distance.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the facility-layout comparison
gates.confirmation: I confirm that facility layouts should be compared with flow-weighted distance when material movement intensity differs among department pairs.

items.label: What failed
items.value: A simple average distance ignored the material-flow pattern.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The highest-flow department pair was also the longest pair in Layout A.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use the total load-distance score Σ(flow×distance).

seo.seo_title: Load-Distance Facility Layout Comparison | FE Industrial E-084
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Industrial & Systems Case E-084: weighted material flow gives Layout B 1300 load-ft/day versus 1600 for Layout A.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Industrial load distance facility layout
seo.excerpt: A layout with shorter average distances can still create more material handling if its highest-flow departments are farther apart.
seo.direct_answer: Layout A has load-distance 50(30)+10(5)+10(5)=1600 load-ft/day. Layout B has 50(20)+10(15)+10(15)=1300 load-ft/day, so Layout B reduces the score by 18.75%.

faqs.a: It is the sum of flow multiplied by travel distance for each relevant origin-destination pair.

faqs.q: Why can average distance be misleading?
faqs.a: It does not weight high-flow department pairs more heavily than low-flow pairs.
